physicsModel.description: Thermal stress (σ) generated in brittle and elastic kitchenware under rapid temperature differential (ΔT), where E is Young's Modulus of Elasticity, α is the linear Coefficient of Thermal Expansion (CTE), and ν is Poisson's ratio.
physicsModel.failureCondition: Catastrophic fracture occurs when localized thermal tensile stress (σ) exceeds the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of the material, typically magnified by microscopic surface flaws and contact thermal conductivity.

materials.name: Tempered Soda-Lime Glass
materials.tradeNames: Modern US Pyrex (lowercase logo), Anchor Hocking, Duralex, Luminarc
materials.composition: 70% SiO₂, 15% Na₂O, 9% CaO (thermally tempered with outer compressive envelope)
materials.acousticProfile: Sudden high-velocity acoustic detonation ('gunshot' snap) as stored compressive energy violently releases.
materials.failurePhysics: Tempering creates a ~10,000 PSI compressive outer envelope over a high-tension core. When an abrupt thermal gradient (ΔT > 55°C) cools the exterior faster than the core, outer contraction generates massive additional tensile stress. If this overcomes the compressive envelope, stored elastic energy detonates the entire matrix into thousands of razor-sharp projectile fragments traveling up to 30 mph.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Extreme. Metal utensils, abrasive scouring pads, and dishwasher rattling produce micro-fissures that act as stress concentration nodes, cutting safe ΔT in half.
materials.safeHandlingTips: Never place a hot dish on a cold, wet, granite, or quartz countertop. Always place hot bakeware on a dry wooden board or cloth potholder. Never add cold liquids to hot glassware in the oven.

materials.name: Annealed Borosilicate Glass (3.3)
materials.tradeNames: Vintage Pyrex (uppercase PYREX, pre-1998 US), European Pyrex, Simax, Duran, Borcam
materials.acousticProfile: Subdued dull 'snap' or ping without projectile shrapnel.
materials.failurePhysics: Borosilicate's boron oxide network exhibits an exceptionally low coefficient of thermal expansion (3.3 vs 9.0 in soda-lime). Because thermal expansion and contraction are minimal, differential cooling generates only a fraction of the internal shear stress. Even when forced to fail under extreme quenching (ΔT > 200°C), it relieves stress via a single linear fracture rather than explosive shattering.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Low-Moderate. Micro-scratches do not catastrophically compromise thermal integrity due to lower bulk stress.
materials.safeHandlingTips: Superb for high-heat roasting and rapid cooling, though physical drops onto tile floors can chip edges more easily than tempered glass.

materials.name: Glazed Ceramic & Stoneware
materials.tradeNames: Le Creuset Heritage Stoneware, Emile Henry, Corningware Stoneware, Fired Pottery
materials.composition: Vitrified aluminosilicate clay matrix sealed with high-fire vitreous glaze
materials.acousticProfile: Metallic crystalline 'pinging' sound as micro-fractures develop across the glaze layer.
materials.failurePhysics: The fired clay body and the surface glaze possess slightly different coefficients of thermal expansion. Under rapid thermal shock (e.g. freezer casserole directly to hot oven, or hot baker into cold dishwater), the outer glaze shrinks or expands faster than the core clay body, producing tensile crazing (spiderweb cracks) followed by deep through-body fracture lines that split the dish in half.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Moderate. Fractured glaze allows grease and wash water to penetrate the porous interior ceramic, breeding mold.
materials.safeHandlingTips: Never move stoneware directly from freezer to preheated oven. Allow frozen meals to thaw to room temperature before baking.

materials.name: Enameled Cast Iron
materials.tradeNames: Le Creuset Dutch Oven, Staub Cocotte, Lodge Enameled, Chasseur
materials.composition: Grey cast iron core (α ~10.5) fused with inorganic vitreous glass enamel coating (α ~8.0)
materials.acousticProfile: Sharp pinging and popping as glass enamel chips fly off the metal substrate.
materials.failurePhysics: Cast iron retains immense thermal mass. Because iron has a higher expansion coefficient than glass enamel, sudden cooling (like pouring ice water into a searing pan) causes the iron substrate to contract much faster than the enamel. This shear force violently pops and 'spalls' flakes of razor-sharp vitreous glass into your food and exposes raw cast iron to rapid oxidation.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Low for iron core, but thermal shock chips in enamel are irreversible and ruin the pot.
materials.safeHandlingTips: Always deglaze hot enameled pots with warm or room-temperature liquids, never ice-cold stock straight from the fridge. Let pans cool before washing.

materials.name: Tri-Ply Clad Stainless Steel
materials.tradeNames: All-Clad D3/D5, Tramontina Tri-Ply, Demeyere, Cuisinart MultiClad
materials.composition: 18/10 Stainless Steel interior/exterior bonded to pure 3003 aluminum thermal core
materials.acousticProfile: Muffled metallic gong or 'oil-can' hollow pop as the pan base permanently buckles.
materials.failurePhysics: Stainless steel is ductile and will not shatter into shards. However, aluminum expands nearly 50% more than stainless steel. When plunged into cold water while searing hot (220°C+), the outer stainless layer contracts instantly while the thick aluminum core resists, warping the base into a convex bowl. The pan becomes a 'spinner' that loses flat contact with glass induction or electric stovetops permanently.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Negligible. Highly resilient to scratching; thermal shock damage is purely mechanical distortion.
materials.safeHandlingTips: Never run cold tap water into a hot stainless skillet immediately after searing. Allow pan to air-cool on the stovetop for 3–5 minutes before cleaning.

materials.name: Pyroceram Glass-Ceramic
materials.tradeNames: Corning Visions (Amber cookware), Pyroceram, Ceran Cooktop Panels
materials.composition: Lithium aluminosilicate glass crystallized with beta-quartz solid solution micro-crystals
materials.shatterMode: Virtually Immune to Culinary Thermal Shock (Mechanical Fracture Only)
materials.acousticProfile: No thermal shock failure under household culinary temperatures.
materials.failurePhysics: Pyroceram was originally developed for military missile nose cones to withstand extreme atmospheric re-entry heat gradients. Its crystal structure has near-zero thermal expansion: heating or cooling produces virtually zero volumetric change. You can take a Pyroceram dish directly from a -18°C freezer and place it over a 300°C open gas flame without thermal fracture.
materials.scratchVulnerability: Low. Resilient to thermal stress, though hard impacts against stone counters can cause standard mechanical chipping.
materials.safeHandlingTips: The ultimate thermal shock-proof kitchenware. Ideal for freezer-to-flame cooking.

contactSurfaces.name: Ice Water Bath (0°C / 32°F)
contactSurfaces.description: Liquid phase immersion provides maximum surface contact area and extreme convective heat extraction, producing the steepest possible thermal gradient.

contactSurfaces.name: Running Cold Tap Water in Sink (15°C / 59°F)
contactSurfaces.description: Flowing tap water rapidly cools one localized section of the cookware while adjacent areas remain boiling hot, generating destructive localized shear stress.

contactSurfaces.name: Cold Granite or Quartz Countertop (18°C / 64°F)
contactSurfaces.description: High thermal conductivity of natural stone (k ~ 3.2 W/mK) acts as a powerful heat sink, chilling the flat bottom while the hot food and upper rim remain expanded, blowing out the base.

contactSurfaces.name: Wet Kitchen Towel or Damp Cloth (20°C / 68°F)
contactSurfaces.description: A very common kitchen mistake: damp towels conduct heat over 20 times faster than dry air and initiate sudden localized evaporative cooling.

contactSurfaces.name: Dry Wooden Board or Silicone Trivet (22°C / 72°F)
contactSurfaces.description: Low thermal conductivity (k ~ 0.15 W/mK) insulates the cookware bottom, allowing gentle, uniform convective cooling without destructive temperature spikes.

contactSurfaces.name: Preheated Hot Oven Chamber (200°C / 392°F)
contactSurfaces.description: Sudden positive thermal shock (+ΔT). Moving chilled or frozen casserole dishes into a hot oven heats exterior surfaces rapidly while frozen center remains rigid.
